docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Stroke is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment. A stroke occurs when the blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted. This protocol outlines the steps for healthcare providers to follow when assessing and managing a patient with suspected stroke.

docs.title: General Guidelines
docs.text:
• Time is Brain: Every minute counts when treating stroke patients. Early intervention can drastically improve outcomes.
  • Primary Goal: Early identification, rapid imaging, and appropriate intervention.

docs.title: Initial Assessment
docs.text:
1. Vital Signs Monitoring
  2. Blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation.

  3. Temperature management is important if fever is present.

  4. Neurological Assessment

  5. FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) test to identify signs of stroke:

    • Face: Ask the patient to smile. Look for drooping on one side of the face.
    • Arm: Ask the patient to raise both arms. Check for weakness in one arm.
    • Speech: Ask the patient to repeat a simple sentence. Check for slurred or abnormal speech.
    • Time: Time is critical. Document the time of symptom onset.

  6. History Taking

  7. Onset of symptoms
  8. Medical history (hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, prior strokes)
  9. Family history of stroke

docs.title: Imaging
docs.text:
1. CT Scan
  2. A non-contrast CT scan is recommended as the first imaging modality to differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.
  3. If hemorrhagic stroke is suspected, initiate appropriate treatment immediately.

  4. If ischemic stroke is suspected, assess the timing and eligibility for thrombolysis.

  5. MRI

  6. MRI is particularly useful for detecting small infarctions and is more sensitive than CT in detecting ischemic stroke.

docs.title: Acute Phase Treatment
docs.text:
1. Thrombolysis (tPA)
  2. If the patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, intravenous thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) may be considered.

  3. Exclusion criteria for tPA:

    • Symptom onset > 4.5 hours
    • Current or recent use of anticoagulants
    • Active bleeding or recent surgery

  4. Mechanical Thrombectomy

  5. Patients with large vessel occlusion who present within 6 hours may be candidates for mechanical thrombectomy, a procedure to physically remove the clot.
  6. Perform thrombectomy within 6 hours of symptom onset for the best outcomes.

docs.title: Post-Acute Care
docs.text:
1. Monitoring
  2. Continuous monitoring in a stroke unit or ICU for the first 24-48 hours.
  3. Neurological checks every 1-2 hours in the initial phase.

  4. Blood pressure management: Avoid hypotension and hypertension.

  5. Secondary Prevention

  6. Initiate antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel) for ischemic stroke patients after ruling out contraindications.
  7. Blood pressure management: Target <140/90 mmHg.
  8. Lipid management: Statins to control cholesterol levels.

  9. Control diabetes and other risk factors.

  10. Rehabilitation

  11. Early mobilization and physical therapy are essential.
  12. Speech therapy may be necessary if the patient has speech or swallowing difficulties.
  13. Cognitive therapy for patients with memory or behavioral issues.

docs.title: Patient Education and Discharge Planning
docs.text:
1. Discharge Considerations
  2. Ensure the patient has appropriate follow-up care with a neurologist.
  3. Provide education on stroke risk factors, prevention, and lifestyle modifications.

  4. Involve family members in the discharge planning and rehabilitation process.

  5. Stroke Prevention Strategies

  6. Encourage smoking cessation.
  7. Promote a healthy diet, regular exercise, and weight management.
  8. Ensure appropriate management of hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Stroke is a time-sensitive medical emergency that requires prompt diagnosis and treatment. Adherence to the stroke protocol improves patient outcomes and reduces long-term disability. Healthcare providers must be prepared to act quickly and follow the guidelines to ensure optimal care for stroke patients.
